power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < 0.20", "p < 0.05", "p < 0.05"
), Text = c("Univariable models were estimated first, and variables with p < 0.20 were entered into the multivariable model.", 
"Crude odds ratios (COR) and adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% CI are reported, and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.", 
"Clusters significant at p < 0.05 are reported.")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p < 0.20 ", Sentence = "Univariable models were estimated first, and variables with p < 0.20 were entered into the multivariable model."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Spatial Distribution and Factors Associated with Unmet Need for Family Planning Among Women of Reproductive Age in Zambia: Evidence from the 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey

author.affiliation:
School of Public Health

									Lusaka

									Lusaka

text.text: Unmet need for family planning contributes to unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions, and preventable maternal and child deaths, and remains high in sub-Saharan Africa.
In Zambia, national estimates may conceal important geographic inequalities.
We assessed the spatial distribution of unmet need for family planning among women of reproductive age in Zambia and the factors associated with it.
We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey (ZDHS), including 12,133 women aged 15-49 years.
We used survey-weighted logistic regression, accounting for the stratified two-stage cluster design, to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).
Global spatial autocorrelation was assessed with Moran's I, local hotspots with the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic, and spatial clusters with a purely spatial Bernoulli scan statistic in SaTScan.
The weighted prevalence of unmet need was 27.0% (95% CI: 25.7-28.3%), ranging from 23.8% in Central to 31.6% in North-Western Province.

Unmet need was spatially clustered (Moran's I = 0.142, p = 0.018), with hotspots mainly in Lusaka, Southern, North-Western, and Northern provinces; SaTScan detected a primary cluster in Lusaka (observed-to-expected ratio 1.42, p < 0.001).
text.formatted: Unmet need was spatially clustered (Moran's I = 0.142, p = 0.018), with hotspots mainly in Lusaka, Southern, North-Western, and Northern provinces; SaTScan detected a primary cluster in Lusaka (observed-to-expected ratio 1.42, p < 0.001).

text.text: Women in union (AOR 2.33, 95% CI: 1.90-2.86) and never-married women (AOR 2.20, 95% CI: 1.69-2.86) had higher odds of unmet need than formerly married women, as did women with five or more children compared with none (AOR 3.05, 95% CI: 2.25-4.13).

Lower odds were observed among women aged 35-49 years (AOR 0.65, 95% CI: 0.52-0.83), women in the richest wealth quintile (AOR 0.62, 95% CI: 0.45-0.86), employed women (AOR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.64-0.84) and urban residents (AOR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.68-0.95).
Unmet need for family planning in Zambia is high, geographically clustered and socially patterned.
Family planning programmes should prioritise hotspot areas, particularly Lusaka, Southern and North-Western provinces, while targeting younger, higherparity and poorer women.
Family planning (FP) is a vital public health intervention that allows women and couples to decide freely whether, when, and how many children to have.
By reducing unintended pregnancies and unsafe abortions, FP improves maternal and child health and contributes to gender equality and socio-economic development [1].
text.formatted: By reducing unintended pregnancies and unsafe abortions, FP improves maternal and child health and contributes to gender equality and socio-economic development <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Unmet need for family planning refers to women who are fecund and sexually active, who wish to postpone or stop childbearing, but who are not using any method of contraception [2].
text.formatted: Unmet need for family planning refers to women who are fecund and sexually active, who wish to postpone or stop childbearing, but who are not using any method of contraception <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: It is a key indicator for monitoring family planning programmes and for identifying barriers to contraceptive access and use.
In 2020, more than 218 million women in low-and middle-income countries were estimated to have an unmet need for contraception [3].
text.formatted: In 2020, more than 218 million women in low-and middle-income countries were estimated to have an unmet need for contraception <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The burden is greatest in sub-Saharan Africa, where the prevalence of unmet need among married women ranges between 22.9% and 26.9% [4], driven by poverty, cultural norms, gender inequalities, and weak health systems [5].
text.formatted: The burden is greatest in sub-Saharan Africa, where the prevalence of unmet need among married women ranges between 22.9% and 26.9% <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, driven by poverty, cultural norms, gender inequalities, and weak health systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: In Zambia, despite steady progress in contraceptive use, about 20% of married women had an unmet need for family planning in the 2018 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey (ZDHS) [2].
text.formatted: In Zambia, despite steady progress in contraceptive use, about 20% of married women had an unmet need for family planning in the 2018 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey (ZDHS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: This persisting gap hinders progress towards Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target 3.7, which calls for universal access to sexual and reproductive health services by 2030.
Unmet need is not evenly distributed within countries.

In Zambia, women in rural and hard-toreach areas face longer distances to health facilities, fewer trained staff, and less exposure to family planning information [6], and provinces such as Luapula and Eastern have previously reported higher levels of unmet need [7].
text.formatted: In Zambia, women in rural and hard-toreach areas face longer distances to health facilities, fewer trained staff, and less exposure to family planning information <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, and provinces such as Luapula and Eastern have previously reported higher levels of unmet need <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Spatial analyses in Uganda and Ethiopia have shown that unmet need concentrates in identifiable geographic hotspots, allowing resources to be directed to highburden areas [8, 9].
text.formatted: Spatial analyses in Uganda and Ethiopia have shown that unmet need concentrates in identifiable geographic hotspots, allowing resources to be directed to highburden areas <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Previous Zambian studies, however, have relied on national and provincial estimates from non-spatial regression models [2, 3, 7], and national averages can mask local inequalities.
text.formatted: Previous Zambian studies, however, have relied on national and provincial estimates from non-spatial regression models <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>, and national averages can mask local inequalities.

text.text: To our knowledge, formal spatial statistics have not yet been applied to georeferenced data from the 2024 ZDHS to locate clusters of unmet need in Zambia.

This study therefore aimed to assess the spatial distribution of unmet need for family planning and to determine the factors associated with unmet need among women of reproductive age (15-49 years) in Zambia, using data from the 2024 ZDHS.
>Materials and methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Materials and methods</head>

text.text: The study analysed data from all ten provinces of Zambia: Central, Copperbelt, Eastern, Luapula, Lusaka, Muchinga, Northern, North-Western, Southern and Western.
Zambia is a landlocked country in southern Africa with a population of approximately 20 million people.
The provinces differ substantially in population density, urbanisation, economic development and access to health services.
This was a cross-sectional study, constituting a secondary analysis of the 2024 ZDHS.
The ZDHS is part of the global Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program and provides nationally representative population and health indicators [10].
text.formatted: The ZDHS is part of the global Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program and provides nationally representative population and health indicators <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: The 2024 ZDHS used a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design.

In the first stage, 545 enumeration areas (EAs) were selected from the national master sampling frame with probability proportional to EA size, after stratification by province and by urban or rural residence (20 sampling strata).
In the second stage, a fixed number of households were selected by systematic random sampling from an updated household listing in each selected EA.
All women aged 15-49 years who were usual residents of, or had slept the previous night in, the selected households were eligible for interview with the Women's Questionnaire.
Data were collected between January and July 2024, and access to the data set was granted and accessed on 15 th December ,2025.
Geographic coordinates of EA centroids, released by the DHS Program with random displacement for confidentiality, were used for the spatial analyses.
For this study, we extracted the pertinent variables from the women's individual recode (IR) file of the 2024 ZDHS.
A total of 13,951 women aged 15-49 years were interviewed in the 2024 ZDHS, and 12,133 women formed the analytic sample

The outcome was unmet need for family planning, derived from the DHS variable v626a and coded as a binary variable (1 = unmet need for spacing or limiting births, i.e., v626a codes 1 and 2;0 = all other codes, including women using contraception).
Consistent with the standard DHS definition, unmet need was present among fecund, sexually active women who wished to delay or limit childbearing but were not using any contraceptive method.
Explanatory variables were selected using an integrated conceptual framework drawing on Andersen's Behavioral Model of Health Services Use [11] and the Social Ecological Model [20].
text.formatted: Explanatory variables were selected using an integrated conceptual framework drawing on Andersen's Behavioral Model of Health Services Use [11] and the Social Ecological Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Predisposing factors were age group (15-24, 25-34, 35-49 years), highest educational level (no education, primary, secondary, higher), and marital status (never married, in union, formerly married).

Enabling factors were household wealth quintile (poorest to richest), employment status (working, not working), place of residence (urban, rural), province, and whether distance to a health facility was reported as a problem (yes, no).
Need factors were parity, measured as the number of living children (0, 1-2, 3-4, 5 or more), and fertility preference (DHS variable v602, entered as a numeric code).
Exposure to family planning messages in the media and ideal number of children were also considered but were not retained in the final model
Data were imported into R from Stata format using the haven package, and variable names were standardised with the janitor package.
Continuous age was grouped into categories, marital status was recoded into three groups, and the number of living children into four groups.
Sampling weights (v005) were divided by 1,000,000 in accordance with DHS guidance.
Two candidate variables had substantial missing data, partner's fertility desire (75.3%) and women's decisionmaking autonomy (46.5%), and were excluded from all models.
Women with missing values on any other model variable were excluded (complete-case analysis).
A sensitivity analysis that retained these two variables with missing-category indicators was performed.
Weighted frequencies and proportions were computed for all study variables.
The weighted prevalence of unmet need and its 95% confidence interval (CI) were estimated nationally and by province.
Survey-weighted chi-square tests were used to assess bivariable associations between each explanatory variable and unmet need.

A complex survey design object specifying clusters, strata, and sampling weights was created with the R survey package (svydesign), and survey-weighted generalised linear models (svyglm) with a quasibinomial family were fitted.
Univariable models were estimated first, and variables with p < 0.20 were entered into the multivariable model.
text.formatted: Univariable models were estimated first, and variables with p < 0.20 were entered into the multivariable model.

text.text: Because women were sampled in clusters, all estimates accounted for the survey design: clustering by EA and stratification were specified in the design object, so that standard errors and confidence intervals reflect the two-stage cluster sampling rather than assuming independent observations.
The EA-level prevalence of unmet need was linked to the geographic coordinates of EA centroids.
Global spatial autocorrelation was tested with Moran's I, using a k-nearest-neighbour spatial weights matrix (k = 5).
Local clusters of high values (hotspots) and low values (coldspots) were identified with the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic at the 95% (|z| ≥ 1.96) and 99% (|z| ≥ 2.58) confidence levels.
Maps were produced with the sf and tmap packages in R version 4.4.1.

As a confirmatory approach based on a different algorithm, spatial scan statistics were applied in SaTScan version 10.1.3 using a purely spatial Bernoulli model, with women with unmet need as cases and women without unmet need as controls.
A circular scanning window with a maximum size of 50% of the population at risk was used, and p-values for the log-likelihood ratio (LLR) were derived from 999 Monte Carlo replications.
Clusters with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant and were mapped in QGIS version 3.42.

text.text: In the adjusted model, marital status and parity were the strongest correlates of unmet need.
Women currently in union (AOR 2.33, 95% CI: 1.90-2.86) and never-married women (AOR 2.20, 95% CI: 1.69-2.86) had higher odds of unmet need than formerly married women.

The odds increased with the number of living children, from AOR 2.04 (95% CI: 1.64-2.54) for 1-2 children to AOR 3.05 (95% CI: 2.25-4.13) for five or more children, compared with women with no children.
Compared with women aged 15-24 years, the odds of unmet need were lower among women aged 25-34 years (AOR 0.70, 95% CI: 0.59-0.82) and 35-49 years (AOR 0.65, 95% CI: 0.52-0.83).

Women in the middle (AOR 0.76, 95% CI: 0.63-0.91), richer (AOR 0.77, 95% CI: 0.61-0.97) and richest (AOR 0.62, 95% CI: 0.45-0.86) wealth quintiles had lower odds than the poorest women, 205 and women with primary education had lower odds than those with no education (AOR 0.76, 95% 206 CI: 0.60-0.96).
Working women (AOR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.64-0.84) and urban residents (AOR 0.80, 207 95% CI: 0.68-0.95) also had lower odds of unmet need.
Each unit increase in fertility preference 208 was associated with higher odds of unmet need (AOR 1.17, 95% CI: 1.10-1.24).
Distance to a 209 health facility was associated with unmet need in the crude analysis but not after adjustment (AOR 210 0.89, 95% CI: 0.78-1.01).

211 After adjustment for individual-level factors, women in Southern (AOR 1.51, 95% CI: 1.15-1.98), 212 North-Western (AOR 1.46, 95% CI: 1.10-1.93), Lusaka (AOR 1.45, 95% CI: 1.13-1.86) and 213 Northern (AOR 1.40, 95% CI: 1.11-1.77) provinces had higher odds of unmet need than women 214 in Central Province.
Sensitivity analyses that retained partner's fertility desire and decision-215 making autonomy with missing-category indicators did not materially change these estimates 216 Table 4.

Statistical 220 significance was set at p < 0.05.221 222 This analysis of the 2024 ZDHS found that more than one in four women of reproductive age in 223 Zambia had an unmet need for family planning, that unmet need was geographically clustered with 224 consistent hotspots in Lusaka, Southern and North-Western provinces, and that marital status, 225 parity, age, household wealth, employment and place of residence were independently associated 226 with unmet need.

text.text: Because the analysis was cross-sectional, these relationships should be 227 interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
The burden observed is consistent with the continuing challenge of unmet need reported across 229 sub-Saharan Africa (4, 13).

Although our estimate is higher than the approximately 20% reported 230 among married women in the 2018 ZDHS [2], the difference should be interpreted cautiously: our 231 analysis included all women of reproductive age rather than married women only, and differences 232 between survey rounds may also reflect measurement, fertility intentions and analytical procedures 233 rather than a true change in unmet need.

text.text: Previous Zambian studies have documented persistent 234 inequalities in contraceptive use and unmet need across socioeconomic and demographic groups [3, 7].
text.formatted: Previous Zambian studies have documented persistent 234 inequalities in contraceptive use and unmet need across socioeconomic and demographic groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: Comparisons across ZDHS rounds should therefore use consistent definitions, denominators and analytical approaches.
The spatial findings add an important dimension by showing that unmet need is geographically patterned rather than randomly distributed.

Similar spatial variation has been documented in Uganda and Ethiopia, where geographic concentration of unmet need has been linked to differences in population characteristics, socioeconomic conditions and access to reproductive health services [8, 9].
text.formatted: Similar spatial variation has been documented in Uganda and Ethiopia, where geographic concentration of unmet need has been linked to differences in population characteristics, socioeconomic conditions and access to reproductive health services <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: The consistency of the findings across Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi* and the scan statistic, together with the elevated adjusted odds in the same provinces, supports the conclusion that geographic context matters, although the three spatial methods are not independent because they rely on the same EA-level data.

The location of the hotspots differs from earlier Zambian reports that emphasised Luapula and Eastern provinces [7], which may reflect change over time, different methods or different populations analysed.
text.formatted: The location of the hotspots differs from earlier Zambian reports that emphasised Luapula and Eastern provinces <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, which may reflect change over time, different methods or different populations analysed.

text.text: Spatial clustering does not establish that place itself causes unmet need, because clustered areas may share unmeasured social, economic or health-service characteristics.
The concentration of unmet need in Lusaka is notable given that urban residence was associated with lower odds at the individual level.
These findings are not necessarily contradictory, because an urban classification can conceal substantial heterogeneity.

Women living in the same city may experience very different access to family planning depending on poverty, settlement characteristics, mobility, information, and service availability [14, 15], and proximity to an urban centre does not necessarily translate into adequate family planning information or effective access in informal settlements [16].
text.formatted: Women living in the same city may experience very different access to family planning depending on poverty, settlement characteristics, mobility, information, and service availability <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">15]</ref>, and proximity to an urban centre does not necessarily translate into adequate family planning information or effective access in informal settlements <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[16]</ref>.

text.text: The Lusaka cluster may therefore point to intra-urban, possibly periurban, inequalities.
Because settlement type and facility accessibility were not measured, this explanation remains a hypothesis for further study.
Younger women had higher odds of unmet need than older women, consistent with evidence from sub-Saharan Africa that young women face distinctive barriers to contraceptive access and use [5].
text.formatted: Younger women had higher odds of unmet need than older women, consistent with evidence from sub-Saharan Africa that young women face distinctive barriers to contraceptive access and use <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative studies have identified concerns about confidentiality, stigma, provider attitudes, limited information, and fear of judgement as barriers among adolescents and young women [17, 18].
text.formatted: Qualitative studies have identified concerns about confidentiality, stigma, provider attitudes, limited information, and fear of judgement as barriers among adolescents and young women <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">18]</ref>.

text.text: The higher odds among women in union and never-married women, relative to formerly married women, are consistent with variation by relationship status reported in Zambia and elsewhere [7, 13].
text.formatted: The higher odds among women in union and never-married women, relative to formerly married women, are consistent with variation by relationship status reported in Zambia and elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">13]</ref>.

text.text: Partner communication, partner opposition, and women's decision-making autonomy may contribute [2], but these factors could not be examined here because the relevant variables had high levels of missing data.
text.formatted: Partner communication, partner opposition, and women's decision-making autonomy may contribute <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, but these factors could not be examined here because the relevant variables had high levels of missing data.

text.text: The dose-response relationship between parity and unmet need is consistent with evidence that reproductive history shapes family planning requirements, particularly as women seek to space or limit further births [4, 19].
text.formatted: The dose-response relationship between parity and unmet need is consistent with evidence that reproductive history shapes family planning requirements, particularly as women seek to space or limit further births <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">19]</ref>.

text.text: Women with several children may also have experienced contraceptive discontinuation, side effects, or dissatisfaction with methods.
Contacts with maternal, postpartum and child health services may therefore offer important opportunities to identify and address unmet need.

The lower odds among wealthier, educated and employed women are consistent with the role of enabling resources in access to health services [11] and with documented socioeconomic inequalities in contraceptive use in Zambia [3].
text.formatted: The lower odds among wealthier, educated and employed women are consistent with the role of enabling resources in access to health services <ref type="bibr">[11]</ref> and with documented socioeconomic inequalities in contraceptive use in Zambia <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The loss of association with distance to a health facility after adjustment suggests that its crude effect was explained by correlated factors such as residence and wealth.

The main strengths of this study are the use of recent, nationally representative, geo-referenced data; analyses that accounted for the complex survey design; and the combination of three complementary spatial methods with survey-weighted regression.
Several limitations should be considered.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes assessment of temporality and causality.
Second, unmet need is derived from self-reported fertility intentions and contraceptive behaviour and may be affected by recall and social desirability bias.

Third, we excluded partner fertility desire and decision-making autonomy because of high missingness, so residual confounding by relational factors is possible, although sensitivity analyses did not materially change the estimates.
Fourth, parity, marital status, and fertility preference are closely related to the definition of unmet need, so their associations should be interpreted with caution.

Fifth, the random displacement of DHS cluster coordinates may have misplaced some EAs and attenuated local clustering; EA-level prevalence is based on a small number of women per EA, and the scan statistic did not incorporate survey weights or adjust for covariates; area-level patterns should not be interpreted at the individual level.
Finally, a single survey round does not allow trends in the spatial pattern to be assessed.
Unmet need for family planning remains a substantial public health concern in Zambia.
It is geographically clustered, with hotspots in Lusaka, Southern and North-Western provinces, and is concentrated among younger, higher-parity and socioeconomically disadvantaged women.
National averages alone are therefore insufficient to guide family planning programmes.

We recommend that the Ministry of Health and its partners: (i) prioritise the identified hotspot areas, including peri-urban Lusaka, Southern and North-Western provinces, when allocating family planning resources and outreach; (ii) strengthen confidential, youth-friendly contraceptive services for adolescents and young women; (iii) integrate family planning counselling into maternal, postpartum and child health contacts to reach higher-parity women; and (iv) reduce financial barriers to contraception for the poorest households.

Future research should link survey data with information on health-facility readiness, contraceptive availability, service quality, partner dynamics and community characteristics to explain the observed spatial inequalities.
